unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 1! In this unit you will explore the world of fables — short stories that teach us important lessons about life. Fables have been told for thousands of years, passed from generation to generation by storytellers, teachers, and parents. They often use animal characters or simple human figures to show us truths about honesty, courage, kindness, and wisdom. As you work through this lesson, you will read a fable, answer questions about it, learn an important grammar rule called the Present Perfect Tense, and even write your own fable with a clear moral message. Every section builds on the one before it, so take your time and enjoy the journey.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and vocabulary. Read and annotate the source texts. Discuss evidence and language choices. Apply the grammar focus. Draft and revise two to three paragraphs. Present, reflect and complete the quiz.
howToUse: “The Weaver and the Wind” is one text in two parts: read the unit reading (part 1) first, then the close reading (part 2). Then read the three parts of “Voices in the Chamber” in order.
As you read, note the evidence and the language choices you notice — Comprehension and Writing both ask you to use them.
In Speaking, the last task is a four-minute talk on the unit; the five before it build up to it.

readings.title: The Weaver and the Wind, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
In a small village near the coast, there lived a woman named Dina who was known across the whole region for her extraordinary skill at weaving. Her cloths were so beautiful that merchants travelled from distant towns just to buy them. The patterns she created were unlike anything anyone had ever seen, with swirling designs of deep blue and gold that seemed to shimmer in the sunlight. People often said that Dina's fingers moved as if they were guided by the wind itself.
Dina was proud of her talent, and she guarded her methods very closely. Whenever younger women in the village asked her to teach them her techniques, she always refused. "These skills took me many years to master," she would say, shaking her head firmly. "Why should I simply give them away? My knowledge is the very thing that makes my cloth so valuable."
Her neighbour was an elderly man named Zane, who often watched her work from his doorstep. He had lived in the village his whole life, and everyone respected him for his patience and wisdom. "Dina," he said gently one morning, stepping a little closer to her loom, "a river that refuses to share its water slowly becomes a swamp. It grows stale, and in the end it turns useless."
"I am no river, Uncle," Dina replied, with a polite but dismissive smile. "I am more like a deep well, and my water is meant for my own family alone. I have worked hard to fill it, and I will not let strangers take from it." Zane shook his head sadly, but he said nothing more, for he had learned long ago that people must discover certain truths for themselves.
One evening, dark clouds gathered along the horizon. The monsoon winds arrived far earlier than anyone had expected, howling through the village with tremendous force. Dina rushed outside to protect her precious loom, but the wind was simply too powerful for her. It tore through her workshop like a wild animal, snapping the wooden frame and scattering her finest silk threads across the muddy ground. The heavy rain that followed soaked everything it touched. By morning, her workshop lay in ruins, and her loom, her thread, and her finished cloths had all been destroyed.
Dina sat among the wreckage with tears streaming down her face. She had no money to replace her loom, and the silk merchants would not return for many long months. Without her weaving, she had no way to earn a living for her family. For the very first time in her whole life, she felt completely helpless.

readings.title: The Weaver and the Wind, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
To Dina's great surprise, the village women arrived at her door the very next morning. "We cannot weave as finely as you can, Dina," said Sana, a young mother who carried her baby on her hip. "But we can certainly help you rebuild your loom. My husband is a carpenter, and he has already started cutting the wood."
"And I can spin fresh thread for you," added Alina, an older woman with strong, hardworking hands. "It will not be smooth silk, but it will be strong and good." One by one, the villagers offered whatever they could. A farmer brought sturdy planks of wood, and a fisherman donated thick rope for the frame. Even the children joined in, gathering the scattered threads from the bushes and fences where the wind had carried them. By the end of the day, Dina's yard was full of people working side by side.
Within a single week, Dina had a brand-new loom. It was different from the old one, rougher in some places and improvised in others, yet it was sturdy and very well built. The thread that Alina had spun was coarser than silk, but when Dina wove with it, something remarkable happened. The cloth she produced had a completely new quality, for it was thicker, warmer, and far more durable than anything she had made before. It was not delicate silk, but it was truly beautiful in its own honest way.
Dina stood before the finished cloth and felt something shift quietly inside her. She turned to the villagers who had helped her and said, "I have been foolish. For years I kept my skill locked away, believing it was mine alone to protect. But look at what we have made together, something far stronger and more useful than anything I ever created on my own."
She paused, looking at the faces around her. "From this day on, I will teach anyone who truly wishes to learn. My knowledge is not made smaller by sharing it. Instead, it is multiplied." Zane, watching from his doorstep as he always did, smiled broadly. "Now the river flows again," he said, "and the whole village will grow green because of it."
In the months that followed, Dina taught twelve women to weave, and each one slowly developed her own patterns and style. The village became famous not for one weaver, but for many, and their cloths were sold in busy markets right along the coast.
The moral of this fable is simple. A single thread breaks easily, but many threads woven together can weather any storm. Sharing what you know does not make you weaker; it makes your whole community stronger.

readings.title: Voices in the Chamber, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Long before independence, on the coast, the busy port town of Kalimani was ruled by distant foreign powers. A tall flag flew over the old chamber, where the laws were written, but those laws were never made for the local people. Twelve-year-old Kian lived in Kalimani with his younger sister, Zara. Their father worked as a boat builder, and their mother ran a small tea stall down by the shore. Although the family was poor, they always spoke with quiet pride.
"Freedom is not just for kings and rulers," their father often said. "Even a fisherman deserves to be heard." One day, a notice suddenly appeared on the market wall, announcing that officials from the northern parliament would hold a public discussion about new trade laws. "Another law?" Zara frowned. "Without ever asking us again?"
Kian had never once been inside the council chamber, but he had heard many whispers. People said illegal taxes were coming. Others quietly feared a blockade of the coast if the villagers dared to resist. At home that evening, Father sighed heavily. "We've been supplied with little, and asked to give much," he said. Mother nodded and added, "These new laws, none of them reflect our voice."
Kian could not sleep at all that night. He had recently read about emancipation in a borrowed history book, and the ideas would not leave him alone. "I have learned," he whispered into the dark, "that real change always comes from voices, from people who finally refuse to stay silent."
The very next day, a teacher invited her students to take part in a mock parliament event. "Each of you will represent a group," she explained carefully. "Every group must argue for or against ratifying a brand-new trade law." "What does ratification actually mean?" asked Zara, looking puzzled. "It means official approval," said the teacher warmly. "It is the step that makes a rule truly real."
Kian's team was chosen to represent the Union of Local Traders. Another group became the Coastline Confederation, while a third group played the part of the colonial ministers. Before the debate began, Kian spoke to his good friend Aran. "I need you to help me write a speech," he said. "We have to reflect the real lives of our people." "What do you want me to say?" Aran asked. "Tell them," Kian replied firmly, "that we will not accept more laws written without our consent. This is no longer just about trade, but about who we are." The day of the event arrived, and the school hall had been rearranged to look like a real government room.

readings.title: Voices in the Chamber, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Desks had been arranged in a wide circle, and at the front sat the students chosen to act as jurors, who would decide which argument was strongest. Kian stepped into the hall, his heart pounding hard. He looked around and saw his teacher nodding. "Speak your truth," she whispered.
The first group argued firmly in favour of the law. "It will increase our provisions," said their leader. "It will also bring harmony between the rulers and the local people." "But that harmony is forced," Kian answered, when at last it was his turn. "It's not harmony if we are not heard." He lifted a cloth-wrapped item and slowly unrolled it on the desk. "This is an instrument my father uses to measure wood. He taught me that you cannot build what you do not first understand. And yet these officials build laws without ever understanding us."
One of the jurors leaned forward. "What would you do instead?" "I would gather our community elders, market traders, boatmakers, and farmers," Kian said steadily. "I would ask them to reflect on what trade truly means to their families." "Has this ever been done before?" someone asked. "No," Kian admitted. "But it should have been. And it must happen now."
After the event, the teacher clapped warmly. "You have argued with determination and clarity." Later that day, Kian overheard a visiting student say, "That speech changed my perspective. I had never once thought of the law from the bottom." Another student added quietly, "It is a disgrace how long ordinary people were kept out of these decisions."
That night, at home, Kian told his father everything that had happened. "I have spoken," he said. "I told them that a real relationship must always travel in two directions." His father smiled with pride. "You have become a citizen today, Kian, not merely a student."
A week later, the real parliament finally arrived in Kalimani. They held a formal forum inside the council chamber, and Kian and Zara stood at the back with dozens of anxious villagers. One foreign official rose and spoke. "We will now vote to approve the new tariffs." A woman in the crowd stood up at once. "We object!" she shouted. Another voice added, "This is a disgrace! You cannot decide everything entirely alone!" Kian stepped forward bravely. "We demand entry into these talks. If you block our voices, you are building warfare without any guns." One minister frowned. "Children cannot speak in serious legal matters." "But who will live with the consequences?" Zara replied. "We will." Suddenly something shifted. A respected elder rose slowly from his seat. "I have spoken about justice for many years," he said, "but today I will finally practise it. Let them speak, and let them be heard."

readings.title: Voices in the Chamber, part 3
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
In the days that followed, something quite unusual began to happen in Kalimani. The officials agreed to hold three full days of open hearings. One by one, the people entered the chamber and gave their honest testimonies. Fishermen spoke about the waters that had been blocked. Farmers described the unfair taxes they had paid for years. Traders listed the supplies and provisions that had never once been delivered.
One old man held up a battered copper pot. "This was made by a local inventor," he said. "He received no credit, no pay, and no name written anywhere. What would you call that, if it is not simple theft?" Each new voice added a little more pressure, and slowly something inside the old system began to shift. "Have you ever seen anything like this before?" Zara asked her mother that night. "Never," she replied softly. "But I have dreamed of it for a very long time."
Two weeks later, a large parchment was posted outside the market. "By shared vote, the parliament has ratified a revised trade law. Local leaders will now sit on the trade council. The blockades will end, and the tax rules will change. This law reflects your voice." That night, a joyful celebration filled the entire port. Drums echoed across the water, and fishermen danced with lengths of bright cloth waving in the air.
Kian stood quietly beside the tea stall, unsure of exactly what he felt. "I never truly imagined they would listen," he told Zara. "Maybe they never wanted to," she replied thoughtfully. "But in the end they had to. We simply made it impossible for them not to." A visiting scholar came to interview Kian. "Tell me," she said, "what do you think really changed the final outcome?" "It was not one single voice," he answered. "It was many voices, rising together. Not anger alone, but perspective and truth." The scholar smiled and said she would write about this remarkable day. "And I will keep on speaking," Kian said, "because there is still so much more to change. This is only the very first step."
The moral of this story is clear. Freedom begins not with noise, but with knowledge, courage, and many voices joined together in a shared purpose.

comprehension.question: What was Dina known for across the region, and why did merchants travel to her village?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She was famous for her beautiful woven cloths, so merchants travelled from distant towns just to buy them.
comprehension.explanation: This is stated at the start of the passage, where her shimmering blue and gold patterns are described.

comprehension.question: How did Dina answer when younger women asked her to teach them her weaving techniques?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She refused, saying the skills had taken her years to master and that her secret knowledge made her cloth valuable.
comprehension.explanation: Dina guards her methods because she believes sharing them would make her own work less valuable.

comprehension.question: What did Zane mean when he warned that a river which does not share its water becomes a swamp?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He meant that talent or knowledge kept only for yourself grows stale and useless, like still, trapped water.
comprehension.explanation: This is figurative language: the flowing river stands for shared knowledge and the swamp for hoarded talent.

comprehension.question: What did the monsoon storm do to Dina's workshop and loom?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The powerful wind snapped her wooden loom and scattered her silk threads, and the rain left her workshop in ruins.
comprehension.explanation: The storm destroys her livelihood, which sets up the problem the community later helps her solve.

comprehension.question: Name two different things that villagers contributed to help Dina rebuild her loom.
comprehension.correctAnswer: Any two: a carpenter cut the wood, Alina spun new thread, a farmer brought planks, a fisherman gave rope, or children collected threads.
comprehension.explanation: The passage lists several distinct contributions, showing the whole village working together.

comprehension.question: How is the new cloth different from Dina's old silk, and what does this difference suggest?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The coarser shared thread makes thicker, warmer, more durable cloth, suggesting that working together creates something stronger than working alone.
comprehension.explanation: The improved cloth symbolises the strength that comes from cooperation rather than isolation.

comprehension.question: Do you agree with the fable's moral that threads woven together can weather any storm? Give a reason.
comprehension.correctAnswer: A reasoned opinion; a strong answer links the moral to a real situation where people achieved more by cooperating than alone.
comprehension.explanation: This evaluation question asks you to judge the moral and justify your view with a relevant example.

comprehension.question: At the start of Voices in the Chamber, who rules Kalimani, and how do the local people feel about the new trade laws?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Foreign powers rule the port town, and the local people feel angry and unheard because the laws are written without asking them.
comprehension.explanation: The passage shows the family's pride and frustration under laws made for them but never with them.

comprehension.question: What is the mock parliament event, and what does the teacher ask each group of students to do?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It is a classroom debate in which each group must argue for or against ratifying a new trade law.
comprehension.explanation: The event lets the students rehearse arguing a case, which prepares Kian for the real forum later.

comprehension.question: Why does Kian hold up his father's measuring instrument during his speech in the debate?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He uses it to argue that, just as you cannot build with a tool you do not understand, the officials make laws without understanding the people.
comprehension.explanation: The instrument becomes a symbol; Kian turns a simple object into a powerful point about fair government.

comprehension.question: What does Kian's father mean when he tells him he has become a citizen today, not merely a student?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He means Kian has begun to take an active, responsible part in his community instead of staying a silent onlooker.
comprehension.explanation: Becoming a citizen here means speaking up and sharing responsibility for decisions that affect everyone.

comprehension.question: By the end of the story, what finally persuades the parliament to change the trade law, and what lesson does this teach?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Many villagers giving honest testimony together create enough pressure to change the law, teaching that united voices and truth outweigh anger alone.
comprehension.explanation: The ending rewards courage and cooperation, echoing the moral that freedom grows from many joined voices.

grammar.title: What the Present Perfect Tense Shows
grammar.explanation: The present perfect links the past to the present. We use it for life experiences, recent news, and situations that began earlier and still matter now, without saying exactly when they happened.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: We form the present perfect with have or has plus a past participle. Use it for experiences (I have visited three countries), for recent results (She has just finished her homework), and for actions that started in the past and continue now (We have lived here since 2019). The exact time is not important; the connection to now is what matters most.
grammar.commonMistake: Do not add an exact past time such as yesterday or last week to a present perfect sentence, because those fixed times belong with the past simple.
grammar.memoryTip: Ask yourself whether the moment still matters now; if it does, reach for have or has plus the participle.
grammar.practice:
Part A: read five sentences and tick the ones that describe experiences rather than fixed past moments. Part B: rewrite two of them to explain how they still matter today.

Answer key (self-check): this exercise does not print its own five sentences, so check your work with the test below rather than a fixed list. Tick a sentence only if it reports an experience, a very recent result, or something that started earlier and still continues, with no exact time named — for example: 'I have visited three countries', 'She has just finished her homework', 'We have lived here since 2019', and, from this unit's story, 'I have learned that real change always comes from voices' and 'the parliament has ratified a revised trade law'. Do not tick a sentence that names an exact finished moment, such as 'I visited Kenya last year', 'She finished her homework at six o'clock', or the story's 'The monsoon winds arrived far earlier than anyone had expected' one evening, because a fixed time belongs with the past simple, not the present perfect. Part B (model rewrites for two ticked sentences): 'I have learned that real change comes from voices, so I still speak up whenever something feels unfair' explains why the lesson still matters today; 'The parliament has ratified a revised trade law, so the blockades have ended and trade in Kalimani is different from this day on' explains how that result still matters now.
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: How to Form the Present Perfect
grammar.explanation: Every present perfect verb has two parts: the helper have or has, and the past participle of the main verb. Use have with I, you, we and they, and use has with he, she and it.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: The pattern is subject plus have or has plus past participle. For example: I have finished my work; She has spoken to the teacher; They have eaten already. In speech we often shorten the helper, so I have becomes I've and she has becomes she's. Remember that he's can mean he is or he has, so let the word that follows guide you.
grammar.commonMistake: Do not use have with he, she or it; those subjects always take has, so write She has finished, never She have finished.
grammar.memoryTip: Chant the pairs aloud until they stick: I, you, we, they take have; he, she, it take has.
grammar.practice:
Part A: complete six sentences with have or has. Part B: shorten three of your answers into contractions and read them aloud.

Answer key (self-check): the six starter sentences are not printed in this exercise, so use the pattern below to check your own six. Every subject pairs with only one helper: I, you, we and they take have, while he, she and it take has. Model set covering all six subjects: I have finished my homework; You have helped me a lot today; We have learned an important lesson; They have eaten already; He has spoken to the teacher; She has arrived early. Part B (contractions for three of these): I have becomes I've, They have becomes They've, and She has becomes She's, so three finished answers read I've finished my homework, They've eaten already, and She's arrived early.
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Regular and Irregular Past Participles
grammar.explanation: For regular verbs the past participle simply adds -ed, exactly like the past simple. Many common verbs are irregular, so their participles must be learned by heart.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Regular participles: play becomes played, clean becomes cleaned, study becomes studied, stop becomes stopped. Watch the spelling: add only -d after a final -e, change -y to -ied after a consonant, and double a final consonant after a short stressed vowel. Irregular participles must be memorised: eat becomes eaten, write becomes written, go becomes gone, see becomes seen, take becomes taken, speak becomes spoken.
grammar.commonMistake: Do not use the past simple form in place of the participle; write I have gone, not I have went, and She has eaten, not She has ate.
grammar.memoryTip: Keep a short list of tricky participles and test yourself on five fresh ones every day until they feel natural.
grammar.practice:
Part A: sort ten verbs into regular and irregular participles. Part B: write the correct participle for five irregular verbs taken from the unit story.

Answer key: Part A — sort the ten verbs from this concept's own examples: regular participles are play (played), clean (cleaned), study (studied) and stop (stopped); irregular participles are eat (eaten), write (written), go (gone), see (seen), take (taken) and speak (spoken). Part B — five irregular participles taken from this unit's own story, with the sentence each comes from: seen, from 'unlike anything anyone had ever seen' and 'Have you ever seen anything like this before?'; heard, from 'he had heard many whispers'; spoken, from 'I have spoken,' he said; become, from 'You have become a citizen today, Kian, not merely a student'; thought, from 'I had never once thought of the law from the bottom' (base forms: see, hear, speak, become, think).
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Positive, Negative and Question Forms
grammar.explanation: The present perfect can be positive, negative or a question. Negatives add not after the helper, and questions move the helper in front of the subject.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Positive: They have read the fable. Negative: They have not (haven't) read the fable yet. Question: Have they read the fable? Short answers keep the helper: Yes, they have, or No, they haven't. Notice that the past participle never changes across these three forms; only the helper moves or takes not.
grammar.commonMistake: Do not drop the helper in negatives or questions; write Have you finished?, not You finished?, and I have not started, not I not started.
grammar.memoryTip: For a question, flip the helper to the front; for a negative, slot not straight after the helper.
grammar.practice:
Part A: turn four positive sentences into questions. Part B: rewrite four sentences as negatives using haven't or hasn't.

Answer key (self-check): the eight sentences are not printed in this exercise, so use the rule to check your own positives, questions and negatives. To make a question, move have or has in front of the subject; to make a negative, add not (or haven't/hasn't) straight after the helper; the past participle itself never changes. Part A model (positive turned into a question): Kian has written a speech becomes Has Kian written a speech?; Zara has asked a difficult question becomes Has Zara asked a difficult question?; the villagers have rebuilt the loom becomes Have the villagers rebuilt the loom?; Dina has taught the women to weave becomes Has Dina taught the women to weave? Part B model (positive turned into a negative): The teacher has given her feedback becomes The teacher hasn't given her feedback; The students have practised their speeches becomes The students haven't practised their speeches; The officials have listened to the fishermen becomes The officials haven't listened to the fishermen; Dina has finished the new loom becomes Dina hasn't finished the new loom.
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Time Markers and Present Perfect versus Past Simple
grammar.explanation: Signal words such as ever, never, already, yet, just, since and for often appear with the present perfect. Choosing between the present perfect and the past simple depends on whether an exact time is fixed.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Use since with a point in time (since 2019) and for with a length of time (for three years). Use the past simple when the time is finished and stated, as in I visited my aunt last Saturday, and the present perfect when the time is open or the result still matters, as in I have visited my aunt many times. If you can add a fixed time like yesterday and it still sounds right, choose the past simple.
grammar.commonMistake: Do not confuse since and for; write for three years to measure a length of time and since 2019 to mark a starting point.
grammar.memoryTip: Since points back to one starting moment, while for measures a whole stretch of time from start to finish.
grammar.practice:
Part A: fill six gaps with since or for. Part B: choose present perfect or past simple in four sentences and explain each choice in a few words.

Answer key (self-check): the six gaps and four sentences are not printed in this exercise, so use the rule to check your own: since marks a starting point in time, for measures a stretch of time. Part A model set: Kian has practised his speech for two weeks; the family has lived in Kalimani for many years; Dina has woven cloth since she was a girl; the village has celebrated since the new law was announced; Zane has watched Dina work since that morning; the elders have spoken about justice for many years. Part B (present perfect or past simple, with reasons): 'Dina visited the market yesterday' takes the past simple because yesterday is a fixed, finished time; 'Kian has practised his speech many times' takes the present perfect because no exact time is named and the experience still counts; 'The parliament ratified the law last month' takes the past simple because last month is a fixed time; 'The village has celebrated since the good news arrived' takes the present perfect because the celebrating started at a point in the past and the good feeling continues now.
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Editing Present Perfect Mistakes
grammar.explanation: Careful writers check their present perfect closely. Most errors come from the wrong helper, the wrong participle, a missing helper, or a fixed past time used by mistake.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Correct these common slips: She have finished becomes She has finished; I have went becomes I have gone; I finished already becomes I have finished already; I have seen that film yesterday becomes I saw that film yesterday. Reading each sentence aloud helps you hear whether the helper and participle agree.
grammar.commonMistake: Do not leave out have or has; the sentence I finished my homework already needs a helper, so write I have finished my homework already.
grammar.memoryTip: Proofread in two passes: first check that every helper is correct, then check that every participle is correct.
grammar.practice:
Part A: correct five faulty present perfect sentences. Part B: explain, in one clause each, what was wrong with two of them.

Answer key: Part A — five faulty present perfect sentences corrected, using the mistakes already named in this concept: She have finished becomes She has finished (wrong helper); I have went becomes I have gone (wrong participle); I finished already becomes I have finished already (missing helper); I have seen that film yesterday becomes I saw that film yesterday (a fixed past time needs the past simple, not the present perfect); I finished my homework already becomes I have finished my homework already (missing helper). Part B (what was wrong, in one clause each, for two of them): 'She have finished' pairs the wrong helper with a she subject, which always needs has; 'I have seen that film yesterday' pairs the present perfect with the fixed time word yesterday, which belongs only with the past simple.

teacherNotes.note: Model new language aloud and check meaning before independent work. Make sure a parent or another adult is present whenever learners use a device or an AI tutor. Give specific feedback on complete sentences, text evidence and precise vocabulary.

Point learners to the AI-tutor prompts built into each vocabulary word and task. Remind them that an adult should stay nearby during tutor use, and that the tutor is for practising word meanings, building sentences, checking grammar and improving their own drafts.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Correct pairs: emancipation = being set free from control; blockade = stopping goods getting in or out; chamber = a room for a special purpose; inventor = a person who creates something new; determination = trying hard despite difficulty; ratification = official approval of a law; perspective = a way of thinking about something; harmony = peace and agreement; illegal = not allowed by law; parliament = the group who make laws.

Suggested order: chamber, harmony, blockade, reflect, provisions, disgrace, warfare, parliament, determination, perspective. Accept any order in which each word fits its sentence sensibly and is used only once.

Government and Law: parliament, confederation, ratification. People: inventor, juror, liberator. Abstract Ideas: harmony, emancipation, determination, disgrace. Conflict and Control: blockade, warfare. Accept a clear one-sentence explanation of each heading.

Noun forms: emancipate becomes emancipation; determine becomes determination; ratify becomes ratification; reflect becomes reflection; provide becomes provision. Check that the two learner sentences use the new nouns accurately.

Accept six genuine details drawn from either story, each with a clear explanation of what it reveals about a character, the setting or the moral. Look for evidence quoted or closely paraphrased from the text.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Correct answer: Not allowed by law or rules. The word describes something that breaks the law, like the unfair taxes feared in the story.
Correct answer: A group of people who make the laws for a country. The parliament in the story eventually ratifies a fairer trade law.
Correct answer: A pleasing sense of peace and agreement. Kian argues that forced harmony is not real harmony when people are silenced.
Correct answer: An action to stop people or goods getting in or out. The villagers feared a blockade of the coast if they resisted.
Correct answer: illegal. The passage reads, 'People said illegal taxes were coming.'
Correct answer: citizen. Kian's father says he has become a citizen, meaning he now takes an active part in the community.
Correct answer: instrument. Kian says, 'This is an instrument my father uses to measure wood,' using it as a symbol.
Correct answer: supplied. Father complains, 'We've been supplied with little, and asked to give much.'
Correct answer: harmony. Kian insists, 'It's not harmony if we are not heard.'
Correct answer: perspective. A visiting student admits, 'That speech changed my perspective.'
